```{r setup, message=FALSE}
library(tidyverse)
library(janitor)
library(p8105.datasets)
library(patchwork)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(fig.width = 10, fig.height = 5)
theme_set(theme_minimal(base_size = 12))
```

## Problem 1

```{r}
data("ny_noaa")

weather = ny_noaa |>
  mutate(
    year = year(date),
    month = month(date),
    day = day(date),
    tmax = as.numeric(tmax) / 10,
    tmin = as.numeric(tmin) / 10,
    prcp = prcp / 10
  )

weather |>
  summarise(across(prcp:tmin, ~ mean(is.na(.x)) * 100)) |>
  pivot_longer(everything(), names_to = "Variable", values_to = "Missing (%)") |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 2)
```

The original dataset contains `r nrow(ny_noaa)` rows and
`r ncol(ny_noaa)` columns, with daily observations from
`r n_distinct(ny_noaa$id)` New York weather stations during 1981–2010.
Each row represents a station and date. Variables include station ID,
date, precipitation, snowfall, snow depth, and max/min
temperature. I created separate year, month, and day variables, converted
temperatures to degrees Celsius and precipitation to millimeters, and
kept snowfall and snow depth in millimeters. Missings number is significant:
about 44% of temperature values are missing, compared with about 6% of
precipitation values. The available observations therefore differ across
variables, stations, and dates.

```{r}
weather |>
  filter(!is.na(snow)) |>
  count(snow, sort = TRUE) |>
  slice_head(n = 10) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Snowfall (mm)", "Observations"))
```

Zero is the most common snowfall value, with 2,008,508 observations.
The next most common values are 25, 13, and 51 mm. Zero is common because
most station-days have no snowfall. The frequent positive values are
approximately one inch, half an inch, and two inches, suggesting that
rounding and conversion from measurements in inches contribute to the
observed pattern.

```{r}
monthly_temperature = weather |>
  filter(month %in% c(1, 7)) |>
  group_by(id, year, month) |>
  summarise(mean_tmax = mean(tmax, na.rm = TRUE), .groups = "drop") |>
  filter(!is.na(mean_tmax)) |>
  mutate(month = factor(month, levels = c(1, 7), labels = c("January", "July")))

ggplot(monthly_temperature, aes(x = year, y = mean_tmax, group = id)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.2) +
  facet_wrap(~ month) +
  labs(
    title = "Average daily maximum temperature by station",
    x = "Year", y = "Average maximum temperature (°C)"
  )
```

July is consistently warmer than January. Stations often rise and fall together across years, suggesting shared annual weather patterns, while differences between stations may reflect location and elevation. January shows greater year-to-year variability. There is an unusually low July average temperature around 1988, approximately 14°C. Such unusual averages merit checking the underlying observations and the number of available days.

```{r, fig.width=13}
temperature_plot = weather |>
  filter(!is.na(tmin), !is.na(tmax)) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = tmin, y = tmax)) +
  geom_bin_2d(bins = 60) +
  scale_fill_viridis_c(trans = "log10") +
  labs(
    title = "Daily minimum and maximum temperatures",
    x = "Minimum temperature (°C)", y = "Maximum temperature (°C)",
    fill = "Days"
  )

snowfall_plot = weather |>
  filter(snow > 0, snow < 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = factor(year), y = snow)) +
  geom_boxplot(outlier.size = 0.4) +
  labs(
    title = "Snowfall between 0 and 100 mm",
    x = "Year", y = "Snowfall (mm)"
  ) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 90, hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5))

temperature_plot + snowfall_plot
```
Minimum and maximum temperatures have a strong positive association.
Most observations form a diagonal band, with few extreme values away
from the main concentration. The snowfall distributions are broadly
similar across years, with larger snowfall amounts forming the upper tail.
There is no obvious steady increase or decrease in the typical amount
within this restricted range. These distributions exclude zero snowfall
and amounts of 100 mm or more, so they do not describe annual snowfall
totals or how often snow occurs.


## Problem 2

```{r}
demographics = read_csv(
  "data/nhanes_covar.csv", skip = 4, show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  clean_names() |>
  drop_na() |>
  filter(age >= 21) |>
  mutate(
    sex = factor(sex, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female")),
    education = factor(
      education, levels = c(1, 2, 3),
      labels = c("Less than high school", "High school equivalent", "More than high school")
    )
  )

accelerometer = read_csv("data/nhanes_accel.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  clean_names() |>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("min"),
    names_to = "minute", names_prefix = "min",
    names_transform = list(minute = as.integer), values_to = "mims"
  )

nhanes = inner_join(demographics, accelerometer, by = "seqn")
```

I skipped the four introductory rows in the demographic file, standardized
column names, excluded participants younger than 21 or with missing
demographic information, and labeled sex and education as factors.
I reshaped the activity measurements into minute and MIMS columns and
joined the datasets by participant ID. All original demographic variables
and minute-level activity measurements are kept for eligible participants.
The final dataset contains `r n_distinct(nhanes$seqn)` participants and
`r nrow(nhanes)` rows, with 1,440 minute-level observations per participant.

```{r}
participants = nhanes |>
  distinct(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education)

participants |>
  count(education, sex) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = sex, values_from = n) |>
  knitr::kable(col.names = c("Education", "Men", "Women"))

ggplot(participants, aes(x = sex, y = age, fill = sex)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(title = "Age distributions by sex and education", x = "Sex", y = "Age (years)") +
  guides(fill = "none")
```

The more than high school category is the largest, with 56 men and 59
women. The less than high school category has similar numbers of men and
women (27 and 28), while the high school equivalent category has more men
than women (35 versus 23). Participants with more than a high school
education tend to be younger. In the high school equivalent category,
women have a higher median age than men, while median ages are more similar
between sexes in the other two categories.

```{r}
total_activity = nhanes |>
  group_by(seqn, sex, age, bmi, education) |>
  summarise(total_activity = sum(mims), .groups = "drop")

ggplot(total_activity, aes(x = age, y = total_activity, color = sex)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.6) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  labs(
    title = "Total daily activity by age, sex, and education",
    x = "Age (years)", y = "Total daily activity (MIMS)", color = "Sex"
  )
```

Total activity generally declines with age, although there is significant
variation between participants. The decline is more pronounced in the
less than high school group. Differences between men and women vary by age
and education, so neither sex has consistently higher activity across
all groups. The smooth curves are less reliable near the age extremes,
where fewer observations are available.

```{r}
activity_by_minute = nhanes |>
  group_by(education, sex, minute) |>
  summarise(mean_mims = mean(mims), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(hour = (minute - 1) / 60)

ggplot(activity_by_minute, aes(x = hour, y = mean_mims, color = sex)) +
  geom_line(alpha = 0.3) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", span = 0.2, se = FALSE) +
  facet_wrap(~ education) +
  scale_x_continuous(breaks = c(0, 6, 12, 18, 24), limits = c(0, 24)) +
  labs(
    title = "Average activity over 24 hours",
    x = "Hour of day", y = "Mean activity (MIMS per minute)", color = "Sex"
  ) +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

In all education categories, activity is lowest overnight, increases in
the morning, remains elevated during the daytime, and declines in the
evening. Men and women have broadly similar daily timing. Differences in
activity level depend on the time of day and education category rather
than showing one consistent gap throughout the day. These are group
averages and do not represent every participant's individual pattern.
Women with more than a high school education tend to have higher daytime
activity than men in that category.
